text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

I'm kind of into a little bit of everything, but K-pop is my main thing. My all-time favorite K-pop group debuted just a few years ago. I love their catchy songs, and I know almost every lyric. My coworkers think it's funny that I listen to K-pop! When I'm working, though, I switch to lo-fi or jazz. It helps me focus, and it's perfect with coffee. I also like a few rock bands. Their songs are really emotional, and some of them give me goosebumps. I'd say I'm not picky. If the melody is good, I'll listen to it. Music is basically my daily fuel.

I listen to music pretty much all day long. In the morning, I'm in my car, driving to work with the music turned up. It's the one time I can sing at the top of my lungs! At the office, I put on my earbuds when I'm coding or fixing something. At night, I play music on a speaker while I read or play games. I don't listen to the radio much. I use a streaming app instead, because I can choose any song I want. As for concerts, I don't go often, but I'd love to. I went to one once with a friend, and the energy was unbelievable. I think I should go more often.

I first got into music because of the kids next door. They had a cassette player, and they played ballads and dance songs all day long, so I couldn't help but listen. I was about eight, and I still remember sneaking over to press play on their tape player. They'd yell, "Hey, don't touch that!" Over time, my taste changed. In my teens, I got into rock and bought my own CDs. Then, as the technology changed, I moved from cassettes to MP3 players and then to streaming. These days, my friends introduce me to new K-pop groups. That's how I found my favorite group! So, in a way, music has been a social thing for me from the very beginning.

The park I like to visit is the seaside park near my apartment. It's a long park along the coast, about ten minutes from my home. There's a wide walking path, big trees, and lots of benches that face the ocean. In the middle, there's a small stage where people sometimes perform. There's also a little kiosk that sells coffee and ice cream, which is a big plus for me! On any given evening, you'll see families riding bikes, old couples walking hand in hand, and kids running around. A few people fish by the pier. When the sun goes down, the sky turns orange, and it's just gorgeous. It's the best place to slow down.

A typical day at the park goes something like this. A friend and I go around six in the evening, after dinner. The first thing we do is stop by the kiosk and grab two iced coffees. Then we start walking along the path. We usually chat about work, music, or what to do on the weekend. After about thirty minutes, we find an empty bench and sit down. I put in one earbud and give my friend the other, and we listen to music together. We watch the ships go by and the sun go down. Sometimes we get a cone of ice cream on the way out. Then we walk home slowly. It's simple, but it's the best way to end the day.

One evening last spring, something really special happened. A friend and I were sitting on our favorite bench when a young guy came up to me. He looked super nervous. He whispered, "Excuse me, could you do me a huge favor?" He said he was going to propose to his girlfriend in ten minutes, and he wanted someone to film it. I said, "Of course!" My friend was so excited. So I stood behind a tree with his phone. When his girlfriend arrived, he got down on one knee, and she started crying right away. She said yes! I was filming, but my hands were shaking, and I may have teared up a little. My friend and I clapped like crazy. The couple thanked us a hundred times. It wasn't about me at all, but it was so heartwarming. I still think about it.

Korea has a lot of holidays, but the two biggest are Seollal and Chuseok. Seollal is the Lunar New Year, and Chuseok is the harvest festival in the fall. On both days, people go back to their hometowns to see their families. That's why the roads are packed! A three-hour drive can turn into eight hours. On Seollal, people wear hanbok, bow to their elders, and eat rice cake soup. The kids get money, which they love. On Chuseok, families make songpyeon, which are half-moon rice cakes, and they share a big meal. There are other holidays too, like Children's Day and Buddha's Birthday, but family gatherings are the heart of it all.

When I was a kid, my favorite holiday was Chuseok. Every year, my whole family went to a relative's house in the countryside. It was a small village with rice fields. All the kids would run around the house like crazy. The best part was making songpyeon. An older relative would give each of us a piece of dough, and we competed to see who could make the prettiest one. Mine always looked like a lump! The other kids laughed at me. At night, we sat in the yard and looked at the huge full moon. An older relative told us stories. I remember the smell of steamed pine needles, and the taste of warm songpyeon. Those were the happiest days of my childhood.

My last holiday was Chuseok, just a couple of weeks ago. This year, I decided to stay home to avoid the traffic. I cooked a big meal, and a few friends came over. We had songpyeon, beef soup, and lots of side dishes. After lunch, one of my friends pulled out a Korean board game called yutnori. It's a game where you throw four sticks. We split into two teams: two against two. It got really intense. On the last throw, one of my friends got the best score, and he shouted, "Mo!" That meant my team lost. He did a little victory dance, and everybody burst out laughing. I've never seen him so happy. It was memorable because everyone was together, and the quiet guy turned into a kid.

Hey, it's me. Do you have a minute? I'm writing a report on the tech industry, and I figured you'd be the best person to ask. First, what are the biggest trends in the industry right now?. Interesting. And how is AI changing things?. I see. What skills are most important for people who want to work in tech?. That makes sense. Also, where do you think the industry will be in five years?. Wow, that's helpful. One last thing: do you know any good articles or books I should read?. Awesome. Thanks a million! I owe you a coffee.

Hey, it's me. I'm so sorry, but I have some bad news. I can't make it to our meeting on Friday. A family member fell at home yesterday, and he's in the hospital. He's going to be okay, but I need to stay with him for a few days. I feel awful, because I know you made time for me. But I still need the information for my report, so I have a few ideas. First, could we do a video call next week instead? Or if you're too busy, I could send you my questions by email, and you could answer when you have time. And if that doesn't work, could you point me to a few good articles? Which one works best for you? Again, I'm so sorry. I'll make it up to you, and lunch is on me!

Actually, there's a product I can't stop thinking about. It's a handheld gaming PC, kind of like a game console with a real computer inside. I first heard about it from a coworker. He showed me a video on YouTube, and I was hooked right away. It has a big seven-inch screen, and the controllers are built into the sides. You can play the same PC games that I play at home, but you can take them anywhere. The battery lasts about three hours, and it's about the size of a thick tablet. What really got me is that I could play on the couch or even on a business trip! Of course, it isn't cheap. It costs about as much as a decent laptop. My friend said, "You already have a computer!" But I'm still thinking about it. It's every gamer's dream.

Honestly, it has changed a lot. When I was a kid, my mom did all the shopping at the traditional market and little shops in the neighborhood. She'd go every day or two, and she knew all the vendors. She'd say, "Give me a little extra!" and haggle for a better price. It was a lot of work. Now, things are totally different. Big supermarkets and convenience stores are everywhere. And more and more people shop online. I order groceries on my phone at 11 p.m., and they arrive at my door before 7 the next morning! I think it's incredible. It's super convenient, but I miss the warmth of the old market. There's something special about picking out your own vegetables.

I remember a news story from last summer that really caught my attention. A bunch of people got food poisoning after eating kimbap they bought at a picnic spot. I think about fifty people ended up in the hospital. It turned out the kimbap had been left out in the hot sun for hours, and the bacteria grew like crazy. The worst part is that kimbap looks totally fine, so nobody noticed anything. After the news came out, the government told stores to check their food more carefully. A few places even had to shut down. The thing is, it could happen to anyone. My family loves going on picnics, so that story made me think. Now I always bring a cooler with ice packs, and I check the expiration date on everything. Better safe than sorry!
